# Collars or No Collars

BROWSE THROUGH ANY TEXT-book on resistance training and you will have no trouble finding directions to use collars when lifting. However, like many principles of resistance training, finding the rationale for doing so can be difficult.

Whether they are referred to as safety pins, locks, or clips, collars are most often used on freeweight barbells as safety measures for preventing plates from slipping or falling off during movement of the bar. Improperly loaded barbells, poor lift technique or instruction, bilateral strength differences, poor motor control, or distractions can cause a compounding “teeter-totter” effect, whereby one side of plates followed by the other may fall off the bar. Obviously, falling plates (even the lightest ones) put participants in dangerous and embarrassing situations.

Some might argue that being able to “throw” the plates off during a missed lift protects the lifter from injury (consider the bench press as an example). This rationale is foolish, however, since such a movement would require at least a minimal level of strength, motor control, and foresight during the failure. This is practically impossible.

Moreover, such an idea strongly suggests that individuals are lifting heavy weights without spotters. Although some lifts can be safely executed without a spotter, fatigued muscles moving free weights demand them if proper technique is to be observed. In addition to participant error, weight room supervisors should remind patrons that heavily used bars, the use of chalk, bar cleaners, and/or lubricants could affect the propensity for plates to slide

Finally, it is no coincidence that the American College of Sports Medicine recommends both the supply and use of collars in its Health/Fitness Facility Standards and Guidelines. Such recommendations may be based on conventional resistance-training practices and limitations on facility management liability.

Use of collars in the weight room is consistent with the gradual, disciplined nature of resistance training. Fitness professionals would do well to instruct participants on the use of collars, the weight room’s ubiquitous safety feature. ▲

The slower, more controlled movements will also allow the muscles to be more involved with the movement of the weight because of the absence of momentum that can be created during faster and more erratic movements. Furthermore, evaluations of proper form and technique can be made more easily if the individual is performing slower movements as opposed to faster ones.

Performing slower, more controlled movements can also reduce the chance of injury. A spotter will be better able to foresee, react, and correct any problems that may arise if the weight is being moved at a slower rate.

Muscular imbalances can also be a problem with novice weight trainers. When first beginning a resistance-training program, one side of the individual may be naturally stronger than the other side. If collars are not permitted to be used, the individual will need to move both sides of the weight at the same time. Therefore, the side of the body that is weaker will be made to keep up with the side that is stronger, and thus help to correct the muscular imbalance.

The absence of collars while performing barbell activities can serve a useful purpose, particularly for those individuals just beginning a resistance-training program. By eliminating the use of collars, proper form and technique can be learned while at the same time correcting muscular imbalances. These aspects of training are sometimes overlooked and can therefore lead to potential injury.
